overview: Early Mataram was the Javanese kingdom of the Borobudur and Prambanan age, with power later centred in East Java. It is distinct from the much later Islamic Mataram. The imported 600-1000 dates are map coverage: 600 precedes its securely documented royal history, and 1000 is no proven fall. Broad polygons reaching across Java, Bali and toward Borneo should not be read as demonstrated control of every island.

periods.title: Temples and endowed communities
periods.summary: The Kalasan inscription documents Panangkaran’s Buddhist foundation and support for learned monks.

periods.title: Royal building and expansion
periods.summary: Kayuwangi and Balitung belong to the period of monumental patronage and expanding eastern connections.

periods.title: A court in East Java
periods.summary: Sindok’s inscriptions locate royal authority in East Java; later political history continues beyond the map cutoff.

sections.title: Kings, learning and the work behind temples

items.text: Under Balitung, who ruled around 898-910, royal charters became more numerous. His authority appears to have expanded into East Java, drawing strength from agriculture and trade. These documents reveal a kingdom organized through grants and local obligations as well as spectacular monuments.

Sindok’s 929 Turyan inscription names his palace Tamwlang. Other charters place his authority around Malang, Surabaya, Mojokerto and Kediri. The political centre had moved east, although recent research suggests that the shift began before his reign.

At Kalasan, an inscription dated 778 records a temple for the Buddhist goddess Tara and accommodation for monks knowledgeable in monastic discipline and Mahayana teachings. Learning required people, buildings and continuing support. This evidence concerns a religious community, rather than schooling available to every child.

The same inscription grants Kalasan village to the monastic community, with regional officials witnessing the gift. It asks future kings to maintain the endowment. Building a temple was only the beginning: someone also had to keep the institution going after its founder died.

The stone opens in Sanskrit: “namo bhagavatyai ārya-tārāyai”, translated by its editor as “Homage to the Noble Lady Tārā!” This is the actual 778 inscription in scholarly Roman transliteration; its original letters use Siddhamatrika script. The greeting gives a small, readable piece of the temple’s devotional world.

sections.title: Mountains of stone and stories on the walls

items.text: Borobudur’s eighth- and ninth-century builders arranged five square terraces below three circular platforms and a great central stupa. Seventy-two smaller openwork stupas surround the upper platforms, each containing a Buddha image. The design makes a whole hillside into a carefully ordered sacred structure.

Borobudur’s changing levels express Buddhist ideas about desire, form and a realm beyond form. Carved walls accompany this ascent. Its architecture combines a terraced mountain with a path toward enlightenment, turning movement through space into part of religious reflection.

At Prambanan, temples honour Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, with shrines for the animals associated with them. Nearby Sewu is Buddhist. Their proximity preserves evidence of different religious institutions sharing the same region; each had its own images, buildings and ritual purposes.

Prambanan’s reliefs tell an Indonesian version of the Ramayana. Carvers translated a long epic into scenes on stone walls. Stories could be encountered visually as well as through spoken or written words, giving visitors characters and events to recognize while moving around the temples.

The temple builders fitted stone blocks together using interlocking construction. Modern restorers have worked with that traditional technique while also adding concrete reinforcement. The buildings visitors see today preserve ancient craftsmanship alongside repairs needed after collapse and earthquakes.

One Borobudur relief shows a market scene associated with fishing and selling the catch. Nets and bamboo fishing equipment appear among the details. These are religious story carvings, but the tools and transactions also offer glimpses of the practical work behind a meal.

Borobudur’s stone musicians play flutes, drums and stringed instruments. One Jataka panel shows people celebrating with drums; other scenes connect music with generosity or the treatment of poor performers. The pictures preserve instruments and social judgments together. Stone is wonderfully durable, but it is not a sound recording.

Ninth- and early tenth-century land charters often list gifts exchanged at ceremonies, including many kinds of cloth. Historian Jan Wisseman Christie used those lists to study textiles that rarely survive intact. An official record can unexpectedly become a guide to what people valued enough to give one another.

At Liyangan on Mount Sindoro’s slopes, archaeologists recovered charred rice, bamboo and wood, together with Chinese ceramics from the Tang period. Food and building materials survive beside imported objects. A handful of burnt grain can tell a different story from a king’s impressive stone inscription.

Liyangan’s excavated remains include irrigated rice fields and wooden houses raised on supports, with woven bamboo walls. These give a more domestic picture of the Mataram era than the great temples do. Stone monuments survived above ground more readily, but many people’s surroundings were built from plants.

A volcanic eruption buried Liyangan beneath falling material and hot flows. Researchers have not found human remains belonging to that eruption, suggesting people may have escaped in time. Its precise date remains debated. The destruction of this settlement should not be mistaken for the sudden end of the entire kingdom.

A later royal inscription, carved in 1041, remembers Queen Isanatunggavijaya as a king’s daughter, a ruler’s wife and a devotee of the Buddha. It also traces Airlangga’s descent through Princess Mahendradatta and Udayana. Royal family history helped explain a new king’s authority; women were central to that remembered lineage.

Modern conservation has added another chapter to Borobudur’s history. The major 1973-1983 restoration reused original material while strengthening the structure and improving drainage. Even a huge stone monument needs help coping with water; keeping rain out of the wrong places is serious heritage work.

ending.text: The imported 1000 endpoint is not the kingdom’s disappearance. East Javanese royal history continued. Airlangga’s 1041 Pucangan inscription looks back on Dharmawangsa’s city burning and on Airlangga taking refuge in the forest before his later rise. This retrospective royal account records a violent political break, followed by renewed kingship. Temples, languages and communities had histories extending beyond a particular court.
